decks.title: Issue and Forfeiture of Shares — Part 1: Issuing Shares for Cash and Other Consideration
goals: Pass journal entries for an issue of shares at par and at a premium, in the journal proper and the cash book
Prepare share capital and related ledger accounts
Record under-subscription, over-subscription and pro-rata allotment
Record shares issued to promoters, underwriters and vendors

slides.heading: Issue and Forfeiture of Shares
slides.body_md: Part 1 — issuing shares for cash, at par and at a premium, the **journal proper and cash book**, **over- and under-subscription**, and shares for **consideration other than cash**. Every company, person and figure in this chapter is imagined.

nodes.label: Shares for consideration other than cash

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the issue process and its entries, the journal proper and cash book, issue at a premium, over- and under-subscription, and shares issued for consideration other than cash
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A company raises its capital by issuing shares under the Companies Act. In this chapter we record that money, from the first application to the last call, and we learn what happens when a shareholder fails to pay. Part one covers issuing shares for cash at par and at a premium, the cash book, subscription problems and shares given for something other than cash.

slides.heading: How a company issues shares
bullets: Each share has a **face value**; money is usually collected in instalments: **application**, **allotment** and one or more **calls**.
Every instalment has its own account, which is first made due and then received.

nodes.label: Allotment: application money becomes capital; allotment money due

visual.alt: Flow of a share issue: the prospectus invites applications, application money is banked, on allotment it becomes capital and allotment money falls due, calls are then made and received, and the shares become fully paid
visual.caption: How a company issues shares for cash

slides.narration: The company publishes a prospectus and invites applications. Applicants send the application money, which the company banks. When shares are allotted, the application money becomes share capital and the allotment money falls due. Later the directors make calls for the rest. Each instalment has its own account, so we can see exactly what has been called and what has come in.

slides.heading: Entries for an issue at par

rows: Bank A/c Dr. To Equity Share Application A/c
Equity Share Application A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c (and To Bank A/c for any refund)
Equity Share Allotment A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c
Bank A/c Dr. To Equity Share Allotment A/c
Equity Share First Call A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c
Bank A/c Dr. To Equity Share First Call A/c

visual.alt: Table of entries for an issue at par: application money received is debited to bank; on allotment the application account is transferred to share capital; allotment and each call are first made due to share capital and then received into the bank

slides.narration: For every instalment we use the same rhythm. When money is due, we debit the instalment account and credit share capital. When money comes in, we debit the bank and credit the instalment account. Application money is the exception: it arrives first, and is transferred to share capital only when the shares are allotted. If all goes well, every instalment account closes at zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Yaman Bicycle Rims Ltd
slides.body_md: Yaman Bicycle Rims Ltd, Phagwara (imagined), issues 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on the first and final call. All shares are applied for and every amount is received.

rows: *(Being application money on 60,000 shares transferred to share capital)*
Equity Share First and Final Call A/c Dr.
*(Being first and final call money due on 60,000 shares)*
To Equity Share First and Final Call A/c
*(Being first and final call money received)*

visual.alt: Journal of Yaman Bicycle Rims Ltd for 60,000 shares of ten rupees at par: application, allotment and first and final call money each received and transferred to equity share capital, totalling 6,00,000

slides.narration: Here is the full journal. Application money is received and transferred. Allotment money falls due and is received, and the same happens for the call. Share capital ends at rupees six lakh, and the bank holds exactly the same amount, because the shares were issued at par and every rupee was paid.

slides.heading: Journal proper and cash book
columns:
**Cash book (bank column)**

- Application money received
- Refunds of application money
- Allotment and call money received

**Journal proper**

- Application money transferred to capital
- Allotment money due
- Call money due

rows: Receipt: To Equity Share Application A/c
Payment: By Equity Share Application A/c
Receipt: To Equity Share Allotment (or Call) A/c

visual.alt: Table showing where each share-issue entry goes when a cash book is kept: money received or refunded through the bank goes to the cash book; the transfer of application money and amounts falling due go to the journal proper

slides.narration: Many companies keep a cash book. Then every receipt or payment through the bank is written in the cash book, not in the journal. The journal proper keeps only the entries that move no cash: the transfer of application money to capital, and the amounts that fall due on allotment and on each call. Together the two books record the issue completely.

slides.heading: Worked example 1 (continued): the cash book
slides.body_md: Journal proper for Yaman: (i) Application A/c Dr. To Share Capital; (ii) Allotment A/c Dr. To Share Capital; (iii) First and Final Call A/c Dr. To Share Capital.

rows: To Equity Share First and Final Call A/c

visual.alt: Cash book, bank column, of Yaman Bicycle Rims Ltd: receipts from application, allotment and the call totalling 6,00,000, closed by a balance carried down of 6,00,000
visual.caption: The journal proper keeps only the three non-cash entries.

slides.narration: With a cash book, Yaman's three receipts appear on the receipts side: application, allotment and the call, totalling rupees six lakh. The balance carried down is the same as the share capital. The journal proper now holds only three entries, the transfer and the two amounts due.

slides.heading: Quick check: face value
slides.body_md: What is the ₹10 on the certificate called?
slides.narration: Recall the name for the value stated in the memorandum and printed on each share.

slides.heading: Issue at a premium: Section 52
slides.body_md: Premium is a **capital receipt**: credit **Securities Premium A/c**, never share capital or profit.

rows: Amount received above face value on an issue of shares
Securities Premium A/c (credit), not share capital
Reserves and Surplus, under Shareholders' Funds
write off preliminary expenses; write off expenses, commission or discount on an issue; provide premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures; buy back own shares
pay dividends (it is a capital receipt)

visual.alt: Table on securities premium under section fifty-two: it is the amount above face value, credited to the securities premium account and shown under reserves and surplus; it may be used for capital purposes such as writing off preliminary or issue expenses, premium on redemption and buy-back, but not for dividends

slides.narration: A company with a good record can issue shares above face value. The extra amount is called securities premium. Share capital is still credited only with the face value, and the premium goes to a separate account. Section fifty-two allows the premium to be used only for capital purposes, such as writing off issue expenses or buying back shares. It can never be paid out as a dividend.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Bageshri Glass Bangles Ltd
slides.body_md: Bageshri Glass Bangles Ltd, Shikohabad (imagined), issues 45,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹13: ₹3 on application, ₹6 on allotment (including the ₹3 premium) and ₹4 on the call. All money is received. Securities Premium A/c is credited with ₹1,35,000.

rows: By Equity Share First and Final Call A/c

visual.alt: Equity share capital account of Bageshri Glass Bangles Ltd: credited with ten rupees per share in three instalments, closing at 4,50,000; the premium of 1,35,000 goes to the securities premium account instead

slides.narration: The premium is due with allotment. When allotment falls due, the allotment account is debited with six rupees a share: three to share capital and three to securities premium. The share capital account therefore collects only ten rupees a share, rupees four lakh fifty thousand in all, while the premium of rupees one lakh thirty-five thousand is kept apart.

slides.body_md: Capital parts of the instalments add up to the face value.

Add the blue parts and you get ten rupees, the face value. Add the yellow part and you get the premium of three rupees.

slides.body_md: Revenue gain or capital receipt?
slides.narration: Decide whether securities premium can ever be treated as a profit of the year.

slides.heading: Over- and under-subscription
bullets: **Minimum subscription:** at least 90% of a public issue must be applied for, or all money is refunded.
**Pro rata:** excess application money is adjusted towards allotment (capital and premium due), and only any surplus is refunded.

rows: Allot the shares applied for; record entries on that number
No allotment; refund all application money
Excess application money adjusted towards allotment (capital, then premium due); surplus refunded or, if the articles allow, held as calls in advance

visual.alt: Table of subscription cases: an under-subscribed issue with at least ninety per cent applied for is allotted on the shares applied for; below ninety per cent all money is refunded; over-subscription is handled by rejecting some applications with refunds, or by pro-rata allotment with the excess adjusted towards allotment and any surplus refunded or held as calls in advance

slides.narration: Applications rarely match the shares offered. If fewer shares are applied for, the company may still allot them, as long as at least ninety per cent of the issue is subscribed; otherwise all money goes back. If more are applied for, the directors can reject some applications, or allot pro rata. With pro rata, the extra money paid is kept towards allotment, and only any surplus is refunded.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: Malkauns Cotton Quilts Ltd
slides.body_md: Malkauns Cotton Quilts Ltd, Kaithun (imagined), offers 50,000 shares of ₹10 at ₹12: ₹4 on application, ₹4 on allotment (including the ₹2 premium), ₹4 on the call. Applications: 85,000 shares. Applications for 10,000 are rejected; the rest get shares pro rata.

visual.alt: Working table for Malkauns Cotton Quilts: 85,000 shares applied for; applications for 10,000 rejected and refunded; the remaining 75,000 allotted 50,000 shares pro rata, so their excess of 1,00,000 is adjusted towards allotment money of 2,00,000

slides.narration: Treat each group separately. The rejected group is refunded rupees forty thousand. The pro rata group applied for seventy-five thousand shares but receives fifty thousand, a ratio of three to two. Their extra application money, rupees one lakh, is exactly half of the allotment money due from them, so it is adjusted, not refunded.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 (continued): the entries
slides.body_md: One transfer entry does three jobs: capital, adjustment towards allotment, refund.

rows: *(Being application money on 50,000 shares transferred to share capital; excess adjusted towards allotment; money on rejected applications refunded)*
*(Being allotment money due on 50,000 shares including premium)*

visual.alt: Journal of Malkauns Cotton Quilts for application and allotment: application money of 3,40,000 received; transferred to capital 2,00,000, adjusted towards allotment 1,00,000 and refunded 40,000; allotment money due including premium, and 1,00,000 received

slides.narration: The application account is cleared in one entry. Four rupees a share on the shares allotted goes to share capital, rupees one lakh is credited to the allotment account, and rupees forty thousand is refunded through the bank. When allotment falls due, the allottees already have credit in the allotment account, so only rupees one lakh more is received.

slides.heading: Shares for consideration other than cash
slides.body_md: Debit what the company **received** (services, commission, an asset or a business); credit share capital and any premium.

rows: Incorporation Costs A/c (or Goodwill A/c) Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c
Underwriting Commission A/c Dr. To Underwriters' A/c; Underwriters' A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c (and Securities Premium A/c)
Sundry Assets A/c Dr. To Vendor's A/c; Vendor's A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c (and Securities Premium A/c)

Business Purchase A/c Dr. To Vendor's A/c; Assets A/c Dr. (Goodwill Dr. or Capital Reserve Cr. as the balance) To Liabilities A/c, To Business Purchase A/c; Vendor's A/c Dr. To Share Capital (and Premium)
Number of shares to a vendor
Amount payable in shares ÷ issue price per share

visual.alt: Table of entries for shares issued for consideration other than cash: to promoters through incorporation costs or goodwill; to underwriters through underwriting commission and the underwriters account; to a vendor through the vendor account, for assets or for a whole business with goodwill or capital reserve as the balancing figure; the number of shares is the amount payable divided by the issue price

slides.narration: Shares need not be paid for in cash. Promoters may receive shares for their work in forming the company. Underwriters may take shares for their commission, which the law limits to five per cent of the issue price, or the rate in the articles if lower. Vendors may receive shares for assets or a whole business. In each case, debit what was received and credit share capital and any premium.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: buying a business with shares
slides.body_md: Darbari Leaf Plates Ltd (imagined) buys the business of Baldev Areca Crafts (imagined) for ₹4,50,000: ₹30,000 by cheque, the rest in equity shares of ₹10 at ₹12.

rows: *(Being business of Baldev Areca Crafts purchased)*
*(Being assets and liabilities taken over; goodwill as the balancing figure)*
*(Being vendor paid by cheque and by 35,000 equity shares of ₹10 at ₹12)*

visual.alt: Journal of Darbari Leaf Plates for the business of Baldev Areca Crafts: business purchase of 4,50,000; assets and creditors taken over with goodwill of 50,000; vendor paid 30,000 by cheque and 35,000 shares at twelve rupees, capital 3,50,000 and premium 70,000

slides.narration: The net assets taken over are worth rupees four lakh, but the price is rupees four lakh fifty thousand, so the extra rupees fifty thousand is goodwill. After the cheque, rupees four lakh twenty thousand is paid in shares at twelve rupees each, which means thirty-five thousand shares. Each share adds ten rupees to capital and two rupees to premium.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: promoters and underwriters
slides.body_md: Bhupali Precision Tools Ltd (imagined) gives 4,000 fully paid shares to its promoters, and pays underwriting commission on a public issue of 80,000 shares at ₹15, at the 4% its articles allow, in fully paid shares at the issue price.

rows: *(Being 4,000 fully paid shares allotted to the promoters for their services)*
*(Being commission at 4% of the issue price due to the underwriters)*
*(Being 3,200 fully paid shares allotted to the underwriters at ₹15)*

visual.alt: Journal of Bhupali Precision Tools: 4,000 shares to promoters debited to incorporation costs; underwriting commission of 48,000 settled by 3,200 shares at fifteen rupees, capital 32,000 and premium 16,000

slides.narration: The promoters' shares are debited to incorporation costs. The commission is four per cent of the issue price, within the legal limit of five per cent, so it comes to rupees forty-eight thousand. It is first credited to the underwriters, then settled with three thousand two hundred shares at fifteen rupees, each carrying five rupees of premium.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Always credited at face value; premium to Securities Premium A/c
Made due (Dr.) and received (Cr.); each closes at nil
Receipts and refunds in the cash book; transfers and amounts due in the journal proper
90% of the issue, or all money is refunded
Excess application money adjusted towards allotment; surplus refunded
Debit what is received (services, commission, assets); credit capital and premium

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: share capital at face value with premium to securities premium; instalment accounts made due and received; cash book and journal proper; ninety per cent minimum subscription; pro-rata adjustment; and shares for consideration other than cash

slides.narration: To sum up: share capital is always credited at face value, and any premium goes to securities premium. Each instalment is made due and then received. With a cash book, receipts and refunds go there and the rest stays in the journal proper. At least ninety per cent must be subscribed. Pro rata excess is adjusted towards allotment. Shares for other consideration debit what was received.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **working** for pro-rata allotment first: shares applied, allotted, money paid, adjusted and refunded.
Split every instalment into **capital** and **premium** before writing the entry.
If the question says a **cash book** is kept, put receipts and refunds there, not in the journal.
Number of shares to a vendor = amount payable in shares ÷ **issue price**, not face value.
Underwriting commission: the **lower** of 5% of the issue price and the articles' rate.
slides.narration: In the exam, write a working note for every pro rata question before the entries. Split each instalment into capital and premium. Watch for the words cash book, and move receipts and refunds there. Divide a vendor's amount by the issue price, not the face value. And remember that underwriting commission can never exceed five per cent of the issue price.

slides.heading: Calls, interest, forfeiture, reissue and disclosure
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **calls in arrears and in advance** with **interest**, **forfeiture** and **reissue** of shares, and the **Schedule III** balance sheet.

nodes.label: Calls in arrears and in advance

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: calls in arrears and in advance, interest on them under Table F, forfeiture of shares, reissue and capital reserve, and disclosure under Schedule Three
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Not every shareholder pays on time. Some pay late, some pay early, and a few never pay at all. In this part we record arrears and advances, with the interest the articles allow, forfeit the shares of defaulters, reissue them, and finally show everything in the balance sheet. One imagined company, Khamaj Solar Lanterns, runs through the whole part.

slides.heading: Calls in arrears

rows: Call money not received on the due date
Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. (with Bank A/c Dr. for the rest) To Equity Share Call A/c
Bank A/c Dr. To Calls in Arrears A/c
Debit balance: money called up but not received
Deducted from subscribed capital in the Note on Share Capital

visual.alt: Table on calls in arrears: unpaid call money is debited to a calls in arrears account; it is cleared when the money is received; the balance is money called up but not received and is deducted from subscribed capital in the note on share capital

slides.narration: When a call falls due and some shareholders do not pay, the unpaid amount is moved into a calls in arrears account. This keeps the call account clean and shows clearly how much is still owed. The balance is a debit: money called up but not received. In the balance sheet it is deducted from subscribed capital.

slides.heading: Calls in advance

rows: Money received before a call is made
Bank A/c Dr. To Calls in Advance A/c
Calls in Advance A/c Dr. (with Bank A/c Dr. for the rest) To Equity Share Call A/c
Credit balance: owed to shareholders until the call is made
Other Current Liabilities (with any interest accrued on it)

visual.alt: Table on calls in advance: money received before a call is credited to a calls in advance account and adjusted when the call is made; the balance is owed to shareholders and is shown under other current liabilities

slides.narration: Sometimes a shareholder pays a call before the directors have made it. That money is not yet share capital, because nothing has been called. It is credited to a calls in advance account, which the company owes to the shareholder. When the call is finally made, the advance is used up against it. Until then it is a current liability.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: Khamaj Solar Lanterns Ltd
slides.body_md: Khamaj Solar Lanterns Ltd, Krishnagiri (imagined), issues 50,000 shares of ₹10 at ₹12: ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (incl. ₹2 premium), ₹4 on the call. Applications for 54,000; 4,000 rejected. Rudra (600 shares) pays neither allotment nor call; Tushita (500) misses the call; Nandita (1,000) pays the call with allotment. The Board waives interest.

rows: *(Being application money on 50,000 shares transferred to share capital; money on rejected applications refunded)*
*(Being allotment money due on 50,000 shares including premium)*
*(Being allotment money received; unpaid amount debited to calls in arrears; later calls received in advance)*
Equity Share First and Final Call A/c Dr.
*(Being first and final call money due on 50,000 shares)*
To Equity Share First and Final Call A/c

sections.heading: 1. Issue of shares at par and at a premium
sections.body_md:
A company issues shares under the **Companies Act, 2013**. Each share has a **face (nominal) value**; share capital is always credited at that value. The money is usually collected in instalments: **application**, **allotment** and **calls**.

**Entries (issue at par)**
- Bank A/c Dr. To Equity Share Application A/c (application money received)
- Equity Share Application A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c (on allotment)
- Equity Share Allotment A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c (allotment money due)
- Bank A/c Dr. To Equity Share Allotment A/c (allotment money received)
- Equity Share First Call A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c; Bank A/c Dr. To Equity Share First Call A/c

**Issue at a premium:** the instalment that carries the premium is split: Equity Share Allotment A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c, To Securities Premium A/c. Under **Section 52**, securities premium may be used only for capital purposes (writing off preliminary expenses, writing off the expenses, commission or discount on an issue of securities, the premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures, buy-back of own securities); never for dividends.

**Check:** capital parts of all instalments = face value; instalment accounts close at nil.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus for this chapter:* bonus shares, rights shares, private placement, sweat equity shares and employee stock option schemes; reservations for small individual participants and minimum tradable lots.

key_terms.definition_md: The nominal value of a share stated in the memorandum; share capital is credited at this amount.

sections.heading: 2. Journal proper, cash book and ledger accounts
sections.body_md:
When a company keeps a **cash book**, every receipt and payment through the bank is recorded in its bank column; the **journal proper** keeps only entries that move no cash.

| In the cash book | In the journal proper |
|---|---|
| Application, allotment and call money received | Application money transferred to share capital |
| Refund of application money | Allotment money due; call money due |
| Arrears and calls in advance received | Forfeiture; transfer to capital reserve |

A mixed entry (application money transferred with a refund) is split: the transfer stays in the journal proper and the refund is a payment in the cash book.

**Ledger accounts:** Equity Share Capital A/c (credit balance = amount called up), instalment accounts (close at nil), Calls in Arrears A/c (debit), Calls in Advance A/c (credit), Securities Premium A/c (credit), Share Forfeiture A/c (credit).

key_terms.definition_md: The journal used for entries that do not pass through cash or bank when a cash book is kept.
The book of original entry for receipts and payments through the bank; its balance is cash at bank.

sections.heading: 5. Over-subscription, under-subscription and pro-rata allotment
sections.body_md:
**Minimum subscription:** a public issue may be allotted only if at least **90%** of it is subscribed; otherwise all application money is refunded.

**Under-subscription** (at least 90%): record every entry on the number of shares actually applied for and allotted.

**Over-subscription:**
1. **Reject** some applications: refund their money.
2. **Pro rata**: excess application money is adjusted towards the money due on allotment (first the capital part, then any premium due); any surplus is refunded, or, if the articles permit, credited to Calls in Advance.
3. A **combination** of rejection, full allotment and pro rata.

**Transfer entry:** Equity Share Application A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c (and Securities Premium A/c if premium is on application), To Equity Share Allotment A/c (excess adjusted), To Bank A/c (refund).

**Working:** shares applied by an allottee = shares allotted × applied ÷ allotted in the group; excess = (applied − allotted) × application money per share.

key_terms.definition_md: The least amount that must be subscribed before a company may allot shares in a public issue: ninety per cent of the issue.
Allotment of shares to applicants in proportion to the shares they applied for.

sections.heading: 6. Forfeiture of shares
sections.body_md:
The directors may **forfeit** the shares of a member who fails to pay a call after notice, as the articles allow. Forfeiture cancels the shares.

**Shares issued at par:** Equity Share Capital A/c Dr. (amount called up) To Calls in Arrears A/c (amount unpaid), To Share Forfeiture A/c (amount received).

**Shares issued at a premium:**
- premium **received**: same entry; Securities Premium A/c is not touched;
- premium **not received**: also Securities Premium A/c Dr. with the premium unpaid (it is cancelled).

**Pro-rata allottees:** excess application money adjusted towards allotment counts as money received, so it is included in the amount forfeited.

**Check:** amount forfeited = money received on those shares − premium received.

sections.heading: 7. Reissue of forfeited shares and capital reserve
sections.body_md:
Forfeited shares may be reissued at par, at a premium or at a discount, as fully paid or partly paid.

- Bank A/c Dr. (price), Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. (discount) To Equity Share Capital A/c (amount credited as paid up), To Securities Premium A/c (any excess over that amount).
- **Limit:** discount per share ≤ amount forfeited per share.
- **Capital reserve:** Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. To Capital Reserve A/c with (amount forfeited on the shares reissued − discount on them).
- The amount forfeited on shares **not yet reissued** stays in the Share Forfeiture Account.

**Working:** forfeited per share × shares reissued − discount = capital reserve.

key_terms.definition_md: Sale of forfeited shares to a new holder, at par, premium or discount.
Reserve created from capital profits, such as the gain on reissue of forfeited shares; not available for dividends.

sections.body_md:
**Balance sheet (vertical form):** I. Equity and Liabilities → 1. Shareholders' Funds → (a) Share Capital (Note), (b) Reserves and Surplus (Note); Current Liabilities → Other Current Liabilities (calls in advance and interest accrued on them).

**Note on Share Capital:** authorised capital and issued capital (for information); subscribed capital split into *subscribed and fully paid up* and *subscribed but not fully paid up*; **less** calls in arrears (calls unpaid); **add** forfeited shares (amount originally paid up).

**Reserves and Surplus:** Securities Premium, Capital Reserve.

**Check:** share capital = Share Capital A/c balance − calls in arrears + Share Forfeiture A/c balance.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Crediting the premium to share capital, or treating it as profit.
- Refunding the whole excess on pro-rata allotment instead of adjusting it towards allotment first.
- Putting receipts in the journal when the question says a cash book is kept.
- Dividing the vendor's amount by the face value instead of the issue price.
- Paying underwriting commission above five per cent of the issue price.
- Debiting Securities Premium on forfeiture when the premium was received.
- Transferring the whole Share Forfeiture balance to Capital Reserve when only some shares are reissued.
- Showing calls in advance as share capital; they are a current liability.
- Taking the wrong period for interest on calls.

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: two or three entries (forfeiture and reissue, interest), or a Note on Share Capital.
- 3 marks: a set of entries for an issue (pro rata, premium, vendor), a cash book with the journal proper, or a balance sheet extract.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 2 + (b) 3: working and entries, entries and a ledger account, or entries and a balance sheet.
- Full practical (practice, 8 marks): working notes 1–2, journal 4–5, ledger account or balance sheet 2. The ISC 2027 weightage for Issue of Shares in Paper I is 11 marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: Bihag Paper Cups Ltd, an imagined company, has a balance of ₹3,00,000 in its Securities Premium Account. For which of these purposes may it NOT use the balance under Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013?

Writing off the commission paid on an issue of its shares
Providing for the premium payable on redemption of its debentures
Paying a dividend to its equity shareholders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Paying a dividend to its equity shareholders. Securities premium is capital, not profit. Section 52 lists capital uses only (preliminary expenses, issue expenses and commission, premium on redemption, buy-back); a dividend is never one of them.

questions.solution_md: List the capital uses allowed by the section; half a mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
Four permitted purposes:
1. Writing off the preliminary expenses of the company.
2. Writing off the expenses of, or the commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of its securities (shares or debentures).
3. Providing for the premium payable on the redemption of its redeemable preference shares or debentures.
